seoTitle: Transfer a Domain From Squarespace to WordPress
metaDescription: Move a domain off Squarespace toward WordPress: whether to send it straight into WordPress.com or through a host like Hostinger, and the EPP code and lock windows that trip people up.
intro: Moving from Squarespace's design constraints toward WordPress's themes, plugins, and custom code is a common upgrade path, and there are two legitimate ways to get the domain there. WordPress.com now accepts a domain transfer directly, provided the domain meets its eligibility rules. The other route, shown in the screenshots below, sends the domain to a general host first — Hostinger in this walkthrough — which is the path people take when they want self-hosted WordPress rather than WordPress.com's own hosting. This guide covers both, plus the authorization code you'll need from Squarespace and the lock windows that can stop a transfer before it starts.
prerequisites: Admin or owner access to the Squarespace account that holds the domain
The domain registered (or last transferred) more than 60 days ago, with no recent change to its contact details

steps.heading: Decide which "WordPress" you're moving toward
steps.body:
WordPress.com, the hosted service, now accepts an incoming domain transfer directly through Hosting Dashboard (or Upgrades) → Domains → Add a domain → Use a domain I own → Transfer your domain name — it isn't blocked the way some older guides describe. The domain still needs to be more than 60 days old and not transferred within the last 60 days, and the transfer is free with an annual paid plan.

Self-hosted WordPress (wordpress.org software running on your own hosting) is a different target, and it's what the rest of this guide follows: you transfer the domain to a general host, then install WordPress there yourself. Pick this path for more control over plugins and server configuration; pick the direct WordPress.com route if you'd rather not manage hosting at all.

steps.heading: Unlock the domain and get its authorization code from Squarespace
steps.body:
In the domains dashboard, open the domain, and toggle Domain Lock off. Click Request transfer code, then confirm with your password or two-factor authentication — Squarespace emails the authorization code (also called an EPP code or transfer key) to the domain's contact address, usually within 24 hours.

Three things can block this before it starts. A domain bought in the last 60 days carries a registration lock. One transferred into Squarespace in the last 60 days carries a separate transfer lock. And a recent change to the domain's contact information can trigger its own short lock. If the transfer code request fails or the toggle won't move, check which of these applies before assuming something's broken.

steps.heading: Start the transfer from your chosen host
steps.body: With the domain unlocked and the code in hand, go to the host you're transferring to — Hostinger in this recording — and start a domain transfer from its dashboard, not from anything inside Squarespace or WordPress.com. Most hosts run seasonal transfer promotions, worth checking, but confirm first that the host actually supports the domain's top-level extension; not every registrar accepts every TLD.

image.caption: The receiving host's homepage — the domain transfer is initiated here, on the host's own site.

steps.heading: Enter the authorization code and choose your name servers
steps.body: The transfer form asks for the domain's Secret Key or Authorization Code (EPP code) under Additional information, then a choice about DNS: use the new host's name servers, or keep the existing ones. Pick the host's name servers if nothing else — email, a CDN — currently depends on this domain's DNS and you want everything to move together. Pick "use existing name servers" if Cloudflare or another service is handling DNS and should stay untouched. Getting this choice wrong doesn't break the transfer itself, but it can knock out email or another service until you fix the DNS afterward.

image.caption: The transfer form's Additional information section, asking for the domain's EPP code and a choice between the new host's name servers or the existing ones.

steps.heading: Submit the transfer and expect a multi-day wait
steps.body: Once submitted, the host confirms the transfer was initiated: it can take up to 5–7 business days to complete, and the domain appears in your domains list once it does. Nothing here is a stalled process on the host's end. Domain transfers involve a handoff between registries and sometimes a confirmation email you need to approve, so a day or two of silence is normal.

image.caption: The transfer-initiated confirmation, noting the 5–7 business day window before the domain shows up in your account.

steps.heading: Point the domain at your self-hosted WordPress site once it lands
steps.body: This step applies to the host-transfer path above; if you sent the domain straight into WordPress.com in step one, it's already connected. After the transfer completes on a host like Hostinger, install WordPress there and point the domain at it — if the domain and hosting now live with the same provider, this can be as simple as attaching the domain to the hosting plan, with no separate DNS step. Give any DNS change some time to propagate before assuming something's wrong if the site doesn't resolve within the first few minutes.

troubleshooting.problem: Squarespace won't unlock the domain or send a transfer code
troubleshooting.cause: The domain is inside a 60-day registration lock (newly bought), a 60-day transfer lock (recently moved to Squarespace), or a short lock triggered by a recent change to its contact details.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the domain's registration, last-transfer, and last-contact-change dates in Squarespace's domains dashboard, then wait out whichever window applies before requesting the code again.

troubleshooting.problem: The authorization code email never arrives
troubleshooting.cause: Squarespace sends it to the domain's registered contact email, which can be out of date or land in spam.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the contact email on the domain in Squarespace before requesting the code again, and check spam folders; contact Squarespace support if it still doesn't show up.

troubleshooting.problem: Email or another service breaks right after the transfer
troubleshooting.cause: The transfer form's name-server choice moved DNS management to the new host, cutting off a service — email, a CDN — that depended on the previous DNS records.
troubleshooting.fix: Recreate the missing DNS records at the new host, or if the domain hasn't transferred yet, redo the request and choose "use existing name servers" instead.

costNote: The transfer itself doesn't cost extra with most hosts, though many run promotional pricing on transferred domains. WordPress.com's direct transfer is free with an annual paid plan; on a free site or monthly plan, it costs the standard renewal price for that TLD. Either way, the domain typically renews for an extra year as part of completing the transfer.

faq.question: Can I transfer my domain directly into WordPress.com?
faq.answer: Yes. WordPress.com now accepts incoming domain transfers directly, provided the domain is more than 60 days old and hasn't transferred in the last 60 days. You still unlock it and get an EPP code from Squarespace first. This guide's screenshots follow the alternate path many people take instead — transferring into a general host to run self-hosted WordPress — which is why a WordPress.com dashboard isn't shown here.

faq.question: Why would I transfer to a host like Hostinger instead of straight into WordPress.com?
faq.answer: Because you want self-hosted WordPress (wordpress.org software) rather than WordPress.com's hosted service — more control over plugins, themes, and server configuration, at the cost of managing hosting yourself.

faq.question: What is the EPP code and where do I find it in Squarespace?
faq.answer: It's the domain's authorization code, also called a Domain Secret Key or transfer key, required by the new registrar to accept the transfer. In the Squarespace domains dashboard, open the domain, toggle Domain Lock off, and click Request transfer code.

faq.question: Why won't Squarespace let me start the transfer?
faq.answer: Most often a lock window: domains bought in the last 60 days, domains transferred into Squarespace in the last 60 days, and domains with a recent contact-info change are all held for a period before they can transfer out.

faq.question: How long does the transfer actually take?
faq.answer: Both WordPress.com and third-party hosts quote roughly 5–7 business days after you submit the request, though the exact timing depends on the registries involved and whether a confirmation email needs approving.
